strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents a coherent end-to-end framework connecting configurable task synthesis, executable symbolic evaluation, and model training. The deterministic judge is preferable to exact-string matching or LLM judging for hypotheses within its supported Prolog fragment.

SLR-Bench provides a useful controlled difficulty structure, varying vocabulary, example count, rule length, background sampling, and rule-generation policy over 20 levels. The evaluation covers a broad range of conventional and reasoning models and reports syntax, task accuracy, token use, and monetary cost.

The results reveal clear empirical trends: accuracy declines with nominal complexity, reasoning models outperform conventional models at substantially greater inference cost, and SLR fine-tuning strongly improves in-domain performance.

The paper is readable, visually polished, and includes helpful examples, formal metric definitions, pricing information, and basic training hyperparameters. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/3e416c83290c45c094fd47aca9240bfb/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not establish recovery of the latent rule or systematic generalization. A hypothesis is counted as solved when it separates the finite examples shown in the prompt; it need not be equivalent to the ground-truth rule, minimal despite the instruction requesting the shortest rule, or correct on unseen worlds. With rich predicates and at most 32 examples, many accidental or instance-enumerating hypotheses may pass. Held-out examples per task, exhaustive equivalence testing over the finite domain, and shortcut analyses are needed before the scores can be interpreted as inductive logical reasoning ability.

The formal account is inconsistent with the implemented task language. The paper describes definite clauses, classical entailment, and function-free Horn logic, whereas LLM-generated rules may use negation-as-failure, disjunction, arithmetic, aggregation, forall/findall, lists, and recursion. These constructs have procedural Prolog semantics and can introduce ordering dependence, floundering, or nontermination. The paper does not specify execution timeouts, safety restrictions, treatment of runtime errors, or a precise accepted grammar. Calling failure to prove a negative example “refutation” also relies on a closed-world assumption not reflected in the formalization.

The claimed curriculum-learning conclusion is insufficiently identified. The only comparison is the original model versus one model trained on ordered synthetic data. There is no shuffled-order control, matched non-curriculum synthetic-data baseline, ablation by tier or generation method, alternative seed, or ordinary fine-tuning control. Consequently, the experiments support a benefit from SLR supervision, but not specifically from curriculum ordering.

Downstream evidence is too weak for the broad generalization claim. Evaluation settings are described only as harness defaults and ambiguously as “few-shot as multiturn”; exact task configurations, prompts, checkpoint selection, decoding parameters, and sample counts are missing. Results are from one training run, lack uncertainty or significance tests, and several reported gains are small enough to be compatible with evaluation variance.

Novelty and leakage controls need stronger validation. Excluding exact test-rule strings does not ensure semantic novelty because rules can be equivalent under variable renaming, literal reordering, or alternate Prolog formulations. The assertion that synthetic generation makes pretraining overlap statistically negligible is also unsupported, especially for common rule templates. Canonicalized semantic deduplication and train-test similarity statistics are needed.

Several broader conclusions are confounded. Model-size comparisons mix model families and training recipes, while the test-time-compute discussion compares different models rather than conducting a controlled compute sweep. Difficulty simultaneously changes many factors, including prompt length, number of examples, vocabulary, sampling policy, and rule family, so declining accuracy does not isolate logical complexity.

Reproducibility is presently incomplete: the code and data are only promised after publication, the LLM used for guided rule generation and its sampling settings are not identified, and the benchmark-generation algorithm has no termination bound or reported rejection rates for rare or impossible class assignments. These omissions prevent independent verification of the benchmark and reported scores.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: constructing scalable, automatically verifiable data for evaluating and training inductive reasoning in LLMs.
The combination of configurable task synthesis, executable Prolog-based evaluation, and curriculum organization is potentially useful infrastructure for NLP reasoning research.
The evaluation covers numerous conventional and reasoning-oriented LLMs and reports syntax, task accuracy, output tokens, and estimated monetary cost rather than accuracy alone.
The manuscript clearly describes the high-level generation pipeline and provides illustrative tasks, formal scoring definitions, curriculum configurations, and some training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not establish recovery of the latent ground-truth rule. OVERALLSCORE merely tests whether a generated hypothesis fits the finite displayed examples; many spurious rules can obtain a perfect score without representing the intended rule or generalizing to new worlds. The instruction asks for the shortest hypothesis, but the symbolic judge neither enforces minimality nor tests semantic equivalence. This substantially weakens claims about correct logical induction and systematic generalization.

There is a serious ambiguity in the validation construction. Figure 6 places the positive target atom itself in the displayed validation program; if this fact is loaded during candidate evaluation, positive queries are trivially entailed independently of the candidate rule. The paper needs executable examples, tests, and a precise account of how positive and negative labels are kept separate from background facts.

The claimed formal scope is internally inconsistent. The method defines generated rules as definite clauses and the limitations describe function-free Horn clauses, whereas LLM-generated examples use negation-as-failure, disjunction, aggregation, arithmetic, lists, forall, cuts, and recursion. These have operational Prolog semantics rather than the stated first-order entailment semantics, and some examples do not match the train representation. Soundness and termination conditions are not discussed.

The downstream results do not support attribution to curriculum learning. Only one tuned model and apparently one run are reported, with no shuffled-order control, same-data non-curriculum control, data-volume control, ordinary instruction-tuning control, variance, or significance analysis. Improvements could therefore arise from additional supervised training rather than the proposed curriculum or improved logical reasoning.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: code and data are promised only after publication; the model used for LLM-guided rule generation is unspecified; decoding parameters, parsing rules, invalid-output handling, random seeds, exact downstream shot settings, and checkpoint-selection procedure are missing. The statement that training uses about 17k examples also appears inconsistent with the stated restriction to the basic, easy, and medium splits and the per-level dataset sizes.

The benchmark's levels simultaneously change rule length, vocabulary, number of examples, number of constants, background distribution, and rule-generation policy. Consequently, declining performance does not isolate logical complexity, and comparisons such as diminishing returns from test-time compute are observational rather than controlled. No ablation validates the proposed difficulty factors or the enormous reported combinatorial-space estimates.

The benchmark uses only 50 test tasks per level, yet reports no confidence intervals, multiple synthesis seeds, or robustness analysis. Differences such as 8.8 versus 8.6 LRL and several small downstream gains are presented as meaningful despite potentially substantial sampling and training variation.

Claims that train/test inputs and outputs are 'completely novel,' that overlap is statistically negligible, and that memorization is avoided are asserted rather than demonstrated. Excluding exact rule strings is insufficient because logically equivalent rules, templates, and closely related backgrounds may cross splits, especially with a small fixed vocabulary and LLM-guided generation.

The compute comparison mixes API prices with estimated prices for locally runnable open models and omits important inference settings and hardware measurements. Completion-token totals vary counterintuitively across model sizes, and cost is not a controlled measure of computational efficiency.

The underlying idea is promising, but the missing semantic-equivalence or held-out-world evaluation, formalism inconsistencies, lack of curriculum controls, and insufficient reproducibility undermine the paper's principal claims. Addressing these issues requires important revisions and new experiments before the work is suitable for Findings.

strengths: SLR addresses an important problem with a coherent end-to-end framework: it synthesizes inductive logic tasks, produces executable validators, and supports both evaluation and supervised or reinforcement-learning workflows without manual annotation.

The benchmark offers useful, controllable variation in vocabulary, rule length, example count, sampling policy, arithmetic, and recursion. The 20-level organization enables substantially finer-grained diagnosis than a single aggregate reasoning score.

The symbolic execution approach is preferable to exact-match or LLM judging for determining whether a proposed rule fits the supplied examples. The evaluation across conventional and reasoning-oriented models also reveals informative accuracy, syntax, token, and monetary-cost trends.

The SLR-tuned Llama results are promising: improvements occur throughout SLR-BENCH and across several external benchmarks, suggesting that synthetic logic training may transfer beyond the generated domain.
weaknesses: The principal validity concern is that the symbolic judge tests only consistency with the finite examples in a prompt, not equivalence to the latent ground-truth rule or performance on fresh instances generated from that rule. Many spurious hypotheses can perfectly fit small tasks—especially levels with only one or two examples—and the judge does not appear to enforce the prompt's shortest-rule requirement. Consequently, OverallScore can overestimate rule induction and systematic generalization. The paper needs ambiguity measurements, held-out-instance evaluation within each task, and shortcut baselines.

The curriculum-learning claim is not causally established. Only one curriculum-trained model is reported, without randomized-order, reverse-curriculum, matched non-curricular synthetic-data, or ordinary continued-training controls. Thus the gains support the usefulness of SLR data, but not the specific conclusion that curriculum ordering causes them.

Experimental uncertainty is not characterized: training apparently uses one run, benchmark cells have no confidence intervals, and downstream gains as small as 0.9–1.9 points are interpreted as consistent generalization without seeds or significance testing. Possible regressions on unreported capabilities are also not assessed.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. Code and data are promised only after publication; the LLM used for generating 30% of later-level rules, its decoding configuration, generation seeds, rule filtering, and key inference settings are unspecified. The appendix also reports training on approximately 17k examples while stating that truncation restricts training to the basic, easy, and medium splits, whose level-wise counts appear inconsistent with that total.

The claimed formal scope is internally unclear. The paper describes function-free definite Horn clauses and first-order entailment, while its LLM-guided rules use Prolog-specific negation-as-failure, disjunction, aggregation, arithmetic, recursion, and built-ins. The operational semantics, termination safeguards, semantic-validity checks, and handling of unsafe or vacuously true rules need precise specification. Likewise, rejection sampling is not guaranteed to terminate for tautological, contradictory, or extremely rare rules.

Broader main-conference claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The instantiation uses one synthetic train domain and single-rule classification, yet the paper claims wide-ranging logical reasoning and arbitrary scalability. Comparisons against closely related synthetic-logic generation or training systems are largely qualitative, and no direct benchmark-quality, diversity, generation-efficiency, or training comparison is provided. These issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the strong idea and promising results.

strengths: SLR addresses a relevant problem: scalable creation and deterministic evaluation of inductive logic tasks without human annotation or unreliable LLM judges.

The synthesis interface exposes interpretable controls over vocabulary, rule length, background sampling, and problem size, and the executable Prolog judge accepts semantically valid alternatives rather than requiring exact string match.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering many conventional and reasoning models, test-time compute, supervised and reinforcement-learning experiments, transfer benchmarks, and qualitative error modes.
The curriculum and per-tier reporting reveal clear performance degradation with increasing task difficulty, while token and monetary-cost measurements provide a useful practical perspective.
The paper is generally readable and includes task examples, formal notation, hyperparameters, prompts, and an extended leaderboard.
weaknesses: The central benchmark does not convincingly measure recovery of the latent rule or systematic generalization. A hypothesis is evaluated on the same positive and negative examples from which it is induced, with no fresh examples sampled from the latent rule. Many extensionally consistent shortcuts can therefore pass without capturing the intended concept, especially at early levels with very few examples. This substantially weakens claims about genuine logical inference and domain-agnostic reasoning.

The stated judge is internally inconsistent with the error analysis: Appendix B.4 says any hypothesis covering all observed positives and rejecting all negatives is correct, whereas grounded label enumeration should satisfy exactly that criterion but is reported as rejected. Any additional hypothesis-language, safety, minimality, or anti-shortcut constraints are not formally specified.

Difficulty is not cleanly isolated. Curriculum levels simultaneously change problem size, vocabulary, rule length, and sampling policies. The parameter ablations compare different pre-existing levels or subsets rather than holding all other factors fixed, so they do not establish causal or precise control of complexity.

The curriculum-order evidence is insufficient: ordered, random, and reverse training obtain LRL scores of 6.01, 5.99, and 5.93, with no multiple seeds, uncertainty, or significance analysis. This negligible difference does not support the stated conclusion that curriculum order matters.

The formal scope is unclear. The paper describes function-free definite Horn clauses, yet LLM-guided examples use negation-as-failure, disjunction, aggregation, arithmetic, universal quantification, and recursion. The recursive example also appears incompatible with the benchmark's train-valued target predicate. The accepted hypothesis language and operational semantics need precise definition and validation.

The downstream-transfer claims rely on single reported runs without uncertainty, matched non-curriculum synthetic-data controls, or controls for additional fine-tuning tokens. Thus improvements cannot be attributed specifically to curriculum learning or latent logical reasoning. Evaluation protocols are vague, and ARC is incorrectly characterized as a symbolic pattern-abstraction task.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: code and data are promised only after publication; generation model/settings, decoding parameters, seeds, epoch or step counts, checkpoint selection, exact evaluation-harness version/configurations, and full GRPO details are missing. The GRPO experiment is especially under-specified and was stopped after reward collapse.

Claims of arbitrary scalability, leakage prevention, and semantic novelty are overstated. The generator uses a finite predefined domain; the reported combinatorial-space calculations and synthesis runtime are unexplained; rejection-sampling efficiency is not analyzed; and only exact rule/background separation, not semantic or template-level separation, is checked.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence: correlations between trace length and failure do not show that verbosity causes derailment, cross-model token counts are not controlled efficiency comparisons, and gains on SLR-Homes alone do not demonstrate domain-agnostic reasoning.

strengths: The core idea—automatically generating ILP-style tasks together with executable symbolic evaluation—is relevant to NLP reasoning research and could support inexpensive, scalable experimentation.

The benchmark exposes a graded collection of synthetic tasks and evaluates a broad range of conventional and reasoning-oriented models. Reporting syntax, semantic accuracy, token usage, and cost provides a useful multifaceted comparison.

The paper includes training experiments on multiple model families, an out-of-domain symbolic dataset, established downstream benchmarks, and a qualitative error taxonomy rather than reporting only aggregate benchmark accuracy.
The presentation is generally clear, and the formalization, generation algorithm, illustrative examples, curriculum table, and training hyperparameters make the intended pipeline understandable.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not establish recovery of the latent rule or systematic generalization. The judge only tests consistency on the finite positive and negative examples appearing in the prompt. Many spurious hypotheses can satisfy these examples without expressing the generating concept. This directly weakens claims about genuine induction and understanding of logical structure; evaluation on newly generated held-out instances from the same latent rule, or semantic equivalence testing over the domain, is needed.

The evaluation specification is internally incomplete. Prompts request the shortest rule, but the formal judge does not enforce minimality. The paper says grounded label-enumeration shortcuts are rejected, although such clauses appear compatible with the stated coverage criterion. Any additional hypothesis restrictions, parser rules, and rejection conditions must be formalized and validated, since they can materially change every leaderboard result.

The claimed controlled difficulty progression changes several factors simultaneously, including vocabulary, number of objects, example count, sampling policy, and rule structure. Several purported ablations are comparisons between curriculum levels and remain confounded: for example, the rule-length comparison also changes problem size, while the mirror-versus-uniform comparison coincides with the introduction of LLM-guided rules. Declining model accuracy therefore does not by itself validate a logical-complexity scale.

Evidence for the curriculum-learning claim is weak. The ordered, random, and reverse results differ only marginally (LRL 6.01, 5.99, and 5.93), no uncertainty or repeated runs are reported, and ordered training is not uniformly best across tiers. The Qwen experiment is explicitly trained with shuffled data yet still improves. Strong claims that curriculum order matters or produces smoother learning are consequently unsupported.

Downstream improvements are based on single before/after fine-tuning comparisons without seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or matched-data controls such as non-curricular synthetic training, generic continued fine-tuning, or shuffled-label/rule controls. Several gains are small, so the evidence does not isolate logical induction as their cause. The broad claim of domain-agnostic reasoning transfer is therefore premature.

The train/test separation guarantee is primarily syntactic: distinct rule strings and backgrounds do not ensure semantic or template-level novelty. The paper acknowledges that semantic independence is difficult but nevertheless claims generalization to entirely new rules and prevention of overlap. Canonicalization, equivalence checks, template-disjoint splits, and explicit similarity analyses are needed.

Reproducibility is not presently adequate. Code and data are only promised after publication, and important details are absent or ambiguous, including the model and decoding configuration used for LLM-guided rule generation, API sampling settings, seeds and run counts, exact output parsing constraints, execution timeouts, and full GRPO configuration. Results from changing proprietary APIs further require archived outputs and versioned artifacts.

Several broad conclusions are based on uncontrolled comparisons. Claims about parameter scaling compare different model families and training recipes, while claims about test-time scaling compare service variants whose internal differences are unknown. Cost comparisons across APIs also conflate pricing, model architecture, caching, and output length rather than measuring a controlled compute intervention.

Some conclusions contradict or overstate the reported evidence: the main text says no models succeed on hard tasks, whereas the leaderboard reports substantial hard-tier accuracy for o3 and GPT-5; correlations between longer outputs and failure are interpreted as derailment without controlling for task difficulty; and the proposed explanation of GPT-5 shortcut behavior in terms of RL objectives is speculative. These issues reduce confidence in the analysis.

Overall, the framework has potential, but the benchmark's construct validity and the causal evidence for curriculum-induced transferable reasoning require important methodological revisions. These concerns prevent a Findings recommendation in the current form, though a substantially strengthened version could plausibly be ready for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: SLR is a relevant and potentially useful end-to-end framework: it generates inductive-logic tasks, executable validators, and training targets with controllable task parameters and no human annotation.
The symbolic evaluation is preferable to exact-match or LLM judging and accommodates multiple hypotheses that fit the supplied examples rather than requiring textual agreement with the latent rule.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering many conventional and reasoning-oriented LLMs, inference cost, pass@k, failure modes, supervised fine-tuning, a preliminary reinforcement-learning experiment, and several downstream benchmarks.

The 20-level benchmark and reported parameter analyses reveal clear performance degradation with increasing task complexity. The framework could support valuable diagnostic and curriculum-learning research.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and candid about limitations such as its synthetic train domain, single-rule tasks, and function-free logic.
weaknesses: The symbolic judge verifies a hypothesis only against the finite positive and negative examples in the prompt, not against unseen instances or semantic equivalence to the latent rule. Especially at early levels with very few examples, spurious hypotheses can receive full credit. This substantially weakens claims that the benchmark measures recovery of logical structure or systematic generalization rather than finite-sample consistency.

The central curriculum-learning claim is not convincingly isolated. The full SLR-tuned model lacks matched controls trained on the same examples in random or reverse order, as well as a comparable non-curriculum synthetic-data baseline. The limited order ablation on levels 5–7 yields nearly identical LRL values (6.01, 5.99, and 5.93), with no multi-seed uncertainty or significance analysis; moreover, the shuffled Qwen training also improves strongly.

The claimed fine-grained control of difficulty is supported mainly by comparisons between different curriculum levels or subsets, where multiple properties can differ. These are not clean interventions on one synthesis parameter. Difficulty is measured through model accuracy rather than an independently justified logical-complexity measure.

The downstream evidence is encouraging but insufficient for strong claims of domain-general reasoning acquisition. Results appear to come from single training runs, without uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or controls for ordinary benefits of additional supervised fine-tuning. Several gains are small, and the large gains require replication.

Leakage and novelty claims are overstated. The paper checks exact ground-truth-rule separation and unique backgrounds but acknowledges that it does not establish semantic separation. Simple rule templates may overlap across splits or with pretraining, and LLM-guided generation further complicates the claim that overlap is prevented.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time: the artifacts are promised only after publication, while important details such as random seeds, repeated-run variability, exact decoding settings, complete prompts for each evaluation condition, and sufficient GRPO configuration details are absent. The RL experiment was also stopped after reward collapse, limiting the claimed generality.

The error analysis lacks a stated sample size, annotation protocol, and reliability assessment. Its output-length correlation is heavily confounded by model family and task difficulty, so it does not by itself show that verbosity causes reasoning derailment.

Overall, the framework is interesting and the experiments are substantial, but unresolved construct-validity and experimental-control issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current version. A next-cycle revision could plausibly address these concerns with per-task held-out semantic evaluation, controlled curriculum baselines, repeated runs, and released artifacts.
